questions.question: Which one of these shapes is a polygon?
options: A half-moon shape with one straight edge and one curved edge
A closed round shape with no straight sides at all
A closed shape made of 4 straight sides, like a hockey card
Three straight sides with a gap left open at one corner
questions.explain: A polygon must be closed AND have every side straight, so the closed 4-straight-sided shape is the only one. The most common trap is picking the half-moon because it has one straight edge — a single curved side is enough to disqualify a shape.

questions.question: Which shape is a regular polygon?
options: A triangle with all 3 sides 5 cm and all 3 angles the same size
A rectangle 8 cm long and 3 cm wide with 4 square corners
A triangle with sides 4 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm
A 5-sided shape with sides 2 cm, 3 cm, 3 cm, 4 cm and 2 cm
questions.explain: Regular means BOTH all sides equal and all angles equal, which only the 5 cm triangle has. The usual trap is choosing the rectangle because its 4 corners look neat and equal — but its sides are 8 cm and 3 cm, so it is irregular.

questions.question: Emma folds a square paper napkin so the two halves land exactly on top of each other. How many different lines of symmetry does a square have?
questions.explain: A square folds 4 ways: one up-and-down, one side-to-side, and one along each diagonal, so the answer is 4. Most students stop at 2 because they only try the two folds through the middles of the sides and forget the corner-to-corner folds.

questions.question: Noah is drawing a symmetric butterfly on grid paper. The fold line runs straight down the middle. He shades 7 squares for the left wing, plus 2 squares for the body that sit right ON the fold line. When he finishes the right wing so the design has line symmetry, how many squares are shaded altogether?
options: 9 squares
16 squares
18 squares
14 squares
questions.explain: Mirror the 7 wing squares to get 7 + 7 = 14, then add the 2 body squares that sit on the fold line, giving 16. The big trap is doubling the body squares too (getting 18) — squares sitting on the line of symmetry are their own mirror image and are counted only once.

questions.question: A splash-pad path is paved with tiles shaped like regular hexagons. One side of a tile measures 7 cm. What is the total distance all the way around one tile?
options: 13 cm
35 cm
49 cm
42 cm
questions.explain: A hexagon has 6 sides, and regular tells you every side is the same 7 cm, so the distance around is 6 x 7 = 42 cm. Common traps are adding 6 + 7 = 13 instead of multiplying, or using 5 sides (35 cm) by mixing up hexagon with pentagon.

questions.question: Sofia is sorting 8 paper cut-outs into a hoop labelled POLYGONS. She has 3 triangles, 2 squares, 1 circle, 1 half-moon (one straight edge and one curved edge), and 1 six-sided figure that has a gap left open at one corner. How many cut-outs belong in the hoop?
questions.explain: Only the 3 triangles and 2 squares are closed with all straight sides, so 3 + 2 = 5 go in the hoop. Watch two traps: the half-moon is not a polygon even though part of it is straight, and the six-sided figure fails because a polygon must be completely closed with no gaps.

questions.question: Aiden is completing a symmetric design on grid paper that is 8 squares wide. The columns are numbered 1 to 8 from left to right, and the line of symmetry runs straight down between column 4 and column 5. Aiden shades a square in column 2. Which column must its matching square be shaded in?
options: Column 5
Column 6
Column 7
Column 8
questions.explain: Measure the distance to the fold first: column 2 is 3 columns to the left of the line, so its mirror must be 3 columns to the right, which is column 7 (the pairs are 1 with 8, 2 with 7, 3 with 6, 4 with 5). The usual mistake is sliding the square across by 4 to land on column 6 instead of measuring from the fold line.

questions.question: Maya's class banner is a rectangle 60 cm long and 40 cm wide. She says it has 4 lines of symmetry, because she can fold it across the middle two ways and also fold it corner to corner two ways, just like a square. How many lines of symmetry does the banner really have?
options: 4 — both middle folds and both corner-to-corner folds match up
2 — only the two middle folds match up, because a corner-to-corner fold lands a 60 cm side onto a 40 cm side
1 — only the fold across the short way matches up
0 — a rectangle has no lines of symmetry unless it is a square
questions.explain: A fold is a line of symmetry only if the two halves land exactly on top of each other, and a 60 cm by 40 cm rectangle passes that test just twice: the up-and-down middle fold and the side-to-side middle fold. The classic mistake is copying the square's 4 lines onto a rectangle — its diagonal fold puts a long side onto a short side, so the halves never match.
